# Model passport, study report and decision {#sec-b27}

## At a glance

**Guiding question:** Which evidence does an independent team need for exactly this target statement?

**For:** project groups, doctoral researchers before a colloquium or submission, reviewers and the people who decide
about the next step · **Prerequisites:** accuracy, calibration and denominators (@sec-b06), reading an AI study
(@sec-b07), grouped splits and transfer (@sec-b19); for the decision sheet @sec-b21 to @sec-b25

**In the course:** [W8 · Colloquium and decision](https://r-heller.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w8-colloquium-and-decision.html)
(required); project milestones from
[W3](https://r-heller.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w3-diagnostics-prediction-evidence.html) to
[W7](https://r-heller.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w7-regulation-data-protection-incident.html)
· **Data:** synthetic (the teaching case of @sec-b19, rebuilt in the chapter) · **Core reading time:** about 10 minutes
:::

## Case and decision {#sec-b27-case}

A doctoral researcher presents a spectral tissue classifier at the faculty's research colloquium. The draft abstract
says that the method "identifies tissue class A or B with 100% accuracy". The counter-reviewer, a statistician from
another group, asks three questions: 100% of what – spectra or animals? Were the test spectra taken from animals the
model had already seen? And who is the claim about – further spectra of known animals, new animals of the same species,
or patients? The researcher has the answers, but they are spread over a lab notebook, two scripts and a slide. The
supervisor has to decide whether the abstract can be submitted on Monday and what the next experiment will be. If the
sentence goes out as written, the claim is about recognising known animals; read as a statement about new animals or
people, it is wrong. If the abstract is withdrawn, a useful negative result goes unreported.

## Core reading {#sec-b27-core}

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Core reading** · required for W8 · about 10 minutes · ends before 'Lab'
:::

### One target statement, one passport

A *model passport* is a one-page record that connects a single target statement with the evidence for it: research
question, data, baseline, validation, uncertainty and limits. The target statement says about whom or what the result
is meant to hold – for example "spectra from animals not seen in training, same species, same device". Every other
field is read against it. Model cards [@mitchell2019modelcards] and datasheets for datasets [@gebru2021datasheets]
document models and data for reuse. The passport borrows their idea of a fixed set of fields but is organised around
one claim, because the same model can have a solid passport for one target statement and an empty one for another.

**The key assumption of this chapter is that an entry in the passport counts as evidence only if an independent team
could reproduce it from the stated data, split and code, and if its unit matches the unit of the target statement.** A
result per spectrum does not support a statement about animals; a test on known animals does not support a statement
about new ones. This is the leakage problem of @sec-b19 seen from the reporting side: Kapoor and Narayanan found data
leakage in published machine-learning studies across 17 fields and proposed model information sheets to catch it
[*published*, @kapoor2023leakage].

Every field has one of three states: *filled* (with its source), *open* or *not applicable*. An open field is not a
weakness to hide. It must state which information would close it – a protocol, a measurement, a second data set, a
decision by a named role. A reader can then see at once what is known, what is missing and how expensive the gap is.

### Three rules for filling in

First, every result carries its numerator, its denominator and its unit: "3/6 spectra" and "1/2 animals" are two
different results, and only one of them matches a statement about new animals. Second, every entry names its source –
a script and its checksum, a protocol, a table in a report – so that the counter-review can find it without asking.
Third, an open field is written so that someone else could close it. "Uncertainty: open" helps nobody. "Uncertainty
between animals: open; closed by a pre-specified test on further animals, with the sample size justified as in
@sec-b16" tells the supervisor what the next experiment has to deliver and roughly what it will cost. The same rule
applies to legal and ethical fields: "data protection: open" becomes "legal basis for the reuse of care data: open;
closed by the assessment of the data protection officer, requested on a stated date".

### A separate decision sheet

The passport describes evidence. The *decision sheet* records what is allowed to happen on the basis of that evidence:
ethics, regulation, data protection, security, the responsible roles, the conditions and the date of the next review.
Keeping the two apart prevents a familiar shortcut, in which a good performance figure is read as permission to use a
model. A passport can be excellent and the decision still "not yet"; a passport can be thin and the decision "run the
next experiment", which is often the right outcome of a research project.

### Choosing the reporting path

The passport is not a publication. When the work is written up, the study type determines the reporting guideline,
and the guideline in turn reveals passport fields that are still open (@tbl-b27-reporting-paths).

| Study type | Typical target statement | Reporting guideline | Appraisal of risk of bias | Chapters |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Diagnostic accuracy | "Among patients referred with suspected fracture, the alert has sensitivity … against the reference standard" | STARD-AI [@sounderajah2025stardai] | – | @sec-b07, @sec-b09 |
| Prediction model, development or validation | "In adults admitted to this unit, the model predicts delirium within 72 hours with calibration …" | TRIPOD+AI [@collins2024tripodai] | PROBAST+AI [@moons2025probastai] | @sec-b05, @sec-b06 |
| Early clinical evaluation of decision support | "In a supervised pilot, the tool changes workflow and safety outcomes as follows …" | DECIDE-AI [@vasey2022decideai] | – | @sec-b20 |
| Animal experiment | "In new animals of this species, the measurement separates tissue classes …" | ARRIVE 2.0, Essential 10 first [@percie2020arrive]; TRIPOD+AI items for any prediction model built in the study | 3Rs justification (@sec-b16) | @sec-b10, @sec-b16, @sec-b19 |
| Simulation | "Under these assumptions, a second operating team reduces waiting time by …" | STRESS-DES, -ABS or -SD [@monks2019stress]; ODD for agent-based models [@grimm2020odd] | verification and validation of the model (@sec-b18) | @sec-b15, @sec-b18 |

: Reporting paths by study type. The guideline is chosen by the design that produced the evidence, not by the method
used. PROBAST+AI is a tool for appraising prediction model studies, not a reporting checklist. Unit: study type; no
data. {#tbl-b27-reporting-paths}

Two practical consequences follow. A study can need two guidelines – an animal experiment that builds a classifier
reports the animal side with ARRIVE and the model side with the relevant TRIPOD+AI items. And a guideline describes what
to report, not what counts as good evidence: a complete ARRIVE checklist for a study with two test animals is complete
and still uninformative.

### The counter-review

Before the colloquium, a second group receives only the passport, the code and the synthetic or controlled data access
described in it. They try to reproduce one number from a fresh R session, check whether the unit of each result matches
the target statement, and write at most three findings. The authors answer each finding with a change, a reason or a
new open field. This is the format of W8; it also works as an internal review before submission. The checklists in
[Methods in R: Reporting templates](https://r-heller.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-reporting-index.html) help the second
group to look for missing items quickly.

**Question for the workshop:** Write the target statement of your project in one sentence. Which single field of your
passport would change if the target statement were moved one step further – from known to new individuals, from one
centre to another, or from animals to patients?

## Lab {#sec-b27-lab}

The Lab fills a passport for the teaching case of @sec-b19: four synthetic animals with three spectra each, fictitious
tissue classes A and B, and a deliberately trivial reference rule. The rule returns the class already seen for a known
animal; for an animal it has never seen, it returns the pre-specified default class A. All numbers below come from that
fixed design.

```{r}
#| label: b27-case
spectra <- data.frame(
  animal   = rep(c("T1", "T2", "T3", "T4"), each = 3),   # four fictitious animals
  spectrum = rep(1:3, times = 4),                          # three spectra per animal
  class    = rep(c("A", "A", "B", "B"), each = 3)          # class is a property of the animal
)

# Reference rule: class of a known animal, otherwise the pre-specified default class A
reference_rule <- function(train, test, default = "A") {
  pred <- train$class[match(test$animal, train$animal)]
  pred[is.na(pred)] <- default
  pred
}

# Plan 1: split by spectrum (spectra 1-2 of every animal for training, spectrum 3 for testing)
train1 <- subset(spectra, spectrum %in% 1:2)
test1  <- subset(spectra, spectrum == 3)
correct1 <- sum(reference_rule(train1, test1) == test1$class)

# Plan 2: split by animal (T1 and T3 for training; T2 and T4 are new)
train2 <- subset(spectra, animal %in% c("T1", "T3"))
test2  <- subset(spectra, animal %in% c("T2", "T4"))
hit2 <- reference_rule(train2, test2) == test2$class
correct2 <- sum(hit2)
animal_correct <- tapply(hit2, test2$animal, all)          # an animal counts if all its spectra are correct

overlap1 <- intersect(unique(train1$animal), unique(test1$animal))
overlap2 <- intersect(unique(train2$animal), unique(test2$animal))

# Target values of the teaching case
stopifnot(correct1 == 4, nrow(test1) == 4,
          correct2 == 3, nrow(test2) == 6,
          sum(animal_correct) == 1, length(animal_correct) == 2,
          length(overlap1) == 4, length(overlap2) == 0)
```

The split by spectrum gives 4/4; every test animal was also a training animal. The split by animal gives 3/6 spectra
and 1/2 animals with an empty ID overlap. Uncertainty follows from the denominators. The exact (Clopper–Pearson)
interval for a proportion needs only `qbeta`.

```{r}
#| label: b27-uncertainty
exact_ci <- function(x, n, level = 0.95) {
  a <- (1 - level) / 2
  c(lower = if (x == 0) 0 else qbeta(a, x, n - x + 1),
    upper = if (x == n) 1 else qbeta(1 - a, x + 1, n - x))
}
results <- data.frame(
  test = c("Plan 1: known animals, per spectrum", "Plan 2: new animals, per spectrum",
           "Plan 2: new animals, per animal"),
  correct = c(correct1, correct2, sum(animal_correct)),
  n = c(nrow(test1), nrow(test2), length(animal_correct))
)
results$accuracy <- results$correct / results$n
results <- cbind(results, t(mapply(exact_ci, results$correct, results$n)))
results
stopifnot(abs(results$lower[3] - 0.0126) < 0.0005, abs(results$upper[3] - 0.9874) < 0.0005,
          abs(results$lower[1] - 0.3976) < 0.0005)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-b27-denominators
#| fig-cap: "Accuracy of the reference rule in the teaching case, with exact 95% intervals. Plan 1 tests spectra of animals that were also in training; plan 2 tests two new animals. The middle row treats six spectra as independent although they come from two animals, so its interval is too narrow. Unit: spectrum or animal as labelled; n = 4 synthetic animals, 12 spectra."
#| fig-alt: "Dot-and-interval chart with three rows. Plan 1, known animals per spectrum: 4 of 4 correct, accuracy 100 percent, interval from about 40 to 100 percent. Plan 2, new animals per spectrum: 3 of 6 correct, 50 percent, interval from about 12 to 88 percent, marked as not independent. Plan 2, new animals per animal: 1 of 2 correct, 50 percent, interval from about 1 to 99 percent. Each row uses a different point shape."
#| fig-height: 3.4
library(ggplot2)

results$test <- factor(results$test, levels = rev(results$test))
results$label <- paste0(results$correct, "/", results$n,
                        c("", "  (spectra not independent)", ""))
ggplot(results, aes(x = accuracy, y = test, shape = test)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), width = 0.2, colour = cdsr_colours[["blue"]]) +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = cdsr_colours[["blue"]]) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), vjust = -1.1, size = 3.3) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = cdsr_shapes[1:3], guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = function(x) paste0(100 * x, "%")) +
  labs(x = "Proportion correct (exact 95% interval)", y = NULL,
       caption = "Synthetic teaching case: 4 animals × 3 spectra; reference rule with default class A.") +
  theme_cdsr()
```

### The filled passport

The passport is a table with one row per field. Each field has a status, and every open field states what would close
it. The script builds it from the objects above, so the numbers cannot drift from the analysis.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-b27-passport
#| tbl-cap: "Filled model passport for the teaching case. Unit: field; data status: synthetic teaching case of @sec-b19."
fmt_ci <- function(i) sprintf("%s to %s", cdsr_percent(results$lower[i]), cdsr_percent(results$upper[i]))
passport <- data.frame(
  field = c("Target statement", "Intended use", "Unit of analysis and independent n", "Data",
            "Reference standard", "Baseline", "Candidate model", "Validation", "Result",
            "Uncertainty", "Counter-check", "Limits", "Code and data access", "Artefact"),
  entry = c(
    "Assign class A or B to spectra from animals not seen in training (same fictitious species, device and protocol)",
    "Research only; no clinical or veterinary decision",
    "Animal; 4 animals with 3 spectra each; test set of 2 new animals",
    "Synthetic teaching data (status: synthetic); class is constant within an animal",
    "",
    "Reference rule: class of a known animal, otherwise pre-specified default class A",
    "",
    "Split by animal; ID overlap between training and test: 0",
    sprintf("%d/%d spectra and %d/%d animals correct", correct2, nrow(test2),
            sum(animal_correct), length(animal_correct)),
    sprintf("Per animal %s (exact 95%%); uninformative with 2 test animals", fmt_ci(3)),
    "",
    "One species, one device; no human data; no statement about patients",
    "Code open; data synthetic and generated by the script",
    paste("Script checksum recorded at release (see the decision sheet)")
  ),
  status = c("filled", "filled", "filled", "filled", "open", "filled", "open", "filled", "filled",
             "filled", "open", "filled", "filled", "filled"),
  closes_gap = c("", "", "", "",
                 "Protocol of the reference method (e.g. histology), including blinding to the spectra",
                 "",
                 "Result of a spectral classifier on the same animal-wise split, compared with the reference rule",
                 "", "", "",
                 "Repeat with changed illumination reference and report the change in the result (see @sec-b10)",
                 "", "", "")
)
knitr::kable(passport[, c("field", "entry", "status", "closes_gap")],
             col.names = c("Field", "Entry", "Status", "Information that would close the gap"))

# Every open field names the information that would close it
stopifnot(all(passport$closes_gap[passport$status == "open"] != ""),
          sum(passport$status == "open") == 3,
          !any(passport$status == "filled" & passport$entry == ""))
```

### The decision sheet

The decision sheet sits next to the passport, not inside it. For the teaching case it reads as follows.

| Dimension | Question | Entry for the teaching case | Responsible role |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ethics | Who could be harmed by an overstated claim? | Future animals in a follow-up study planned on a false premise; later patients if the claim travels into a clinical study. The next experiment needs a 3Rs justification (@sec-b16). | principal investigator with the animal welfare officer |
| Regulation | Does the intended purpose make this a medical device or high-risk AI system? | No: research only, no diagnostic purpose. Re-assess if the purpose changes (@sec-b22). | principal investigator |
| Data protection | Are personal data processed? | No (animal data). Would become relevant with human measurements (@sec-b23). | – |
| Security | Is the evaluated artefact the one that is reported? | Checksum of the analysis script recorded; repository access limited to the project group (@sec-b24, @sec-b25). | project data manager |
| Responsibility | Who decides, who reviewed? | Decision: principal investigator. Counter-review: statistician of another group. | named in the project file |
| Decision and conditions | What is allowed now? | Abstract may report the animal-wise result (1/2 animals) and the reference rule; it must not report 4/4 as accuracy. Next step: spectral classifier on new animals with a sample size justified in advance. | principal investigator |
| Review | When is this sheet looked at again? | Before any submission, and after the next experiment; date set by the principal investigator. | principal investigator |

: Decision sheet for the teaching case, kept separate from the passport. Unit: decision; data status: fictitious
project. {#tbl-b27-decision-sheet}

### When an alert goes wrong: who acts next {#sec-b27-faulty-alarm}

In a clinical pilot, the decision sheet has to answer one question that matters most on a bad day: after a faulty or
harmful alert, who acts next? A workable order, to be adapted locally, is the following.

1. The treating clinician decides on the patient's care now, independently of the tool, and documents the alert and
   what was done.
2. The clinician reports the event to the pilot lead named in the decision sheet (row "Responsibility"). In a ward
   pilot this is usually the clinical lead of the unit, not the developer. The pilot lead decides whether the tool
   stays on, runs under stricter conditions or is switched off, using the stop criterion of the monitoring plan
   (@sec-b20).
3. The pilot lead informs the roles the event concerns: the developer or manufacturer for analysis, the person
   responsible for medical device questions if the tool may be a device (@sec-b22), the data protection officer if
   personal data went where they should not (@sec-b23), and information security if manipulation is suspected
   (@sec-b25).
4. The patient is told what happened in words they can follow (@sec-b21).

This order is an *assumption* of the book, not a legal prescription. Who holds each role is decided locally and written
into the decision sheet before the pilot starts; an empty "Responsibility" row is a reason not to start.

### A method-specific short report

The study is an animal experiment that evaluates a classification rule, so the short report follows the ARRIVE
Essential 10 for the animal side and borrows the TRIPOD+AI items on data splitting and performance for the model side.
The text below is generated from the analysis objects.

> **Methods (short report).** Design: synthetic teaching experiment with `r length(unique(spectra$animal))` animals,
> `r nrow(spectra)/length(unique(spectra$animal))` spectra per animal and a class label that is constant within an
> animal (ARRIVE items 1, 6, 8). Sample size: fixed by design; no calculation, because the experiment is didactic
> (item 2; a real study would justify it). Exclusions: none (item 3). Randomisation and blinding: not applicable to
> synthetic data (items 4–5); a real study reports both. Analysis: a reference rule that returns the known class of an
> animal and the pre-specified default class A for new animals; evaluation by an animal-wise split with
> `r length(unique(train2$animal))` training and `r length(unique(test2$animal))` test animals and an empty ID overlap;
> exact 95% intervals (item 7; TRIPOD+AI items on data splitting and performance measures).
>
> **Results (short report).** In new animals the rule classified `r correct2` of `r nrow(test2)` spectra and
> `r sum(animal_correct)` of `r length(animal_correct)` animals correctly (per animal `r cdsr_percent(results$accuracy[3], 0)`,
> 95% interval `r fmt_ci(3)`). A split by spectrum, in which every test animal had been seen in training, gave
> `r correct1` of `r nrow(test1)` spectra correct; this measures recognition of known animals and is not reported as
> accuracy (item 10).

### Counter-review

The second group reads the passport and the code. Their three findings, and the answers, are part of the record.

| Finding | Answer | Status |
|---|---|---|
| The abstract reports 4/4, which comes from plan 1 (known animals). | Abstract changed to the animal-wise result; plan 1 is reported as a recognition check only. | closed |
| The per-spectrum interval for plan 2 treats six spectra as independent. | Interval reported per animal; per-spectrum result kept as description. | closed |
| No candidate model has been evaluated; the reference rule is trivial. | Correct; recorded as an open field with the information that would close it. | open, with plan |

: Counter-review of the teaching passport. Unit: finding. {#tbl-b27-counter-review}

| Dimension | Question | Entry | Responsible role |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ethics | Who bears the harm of a wrong decision, and who can object? | | |
| Regulation | Which intended purpose, which role, which legal text, which open classification? | | |
| Data protection | Which data, which legal basis, which recipients, when deleted? | | |
| Security | Which threat, which control, which test, who reacts? | | |
| Responsibility | Who decides, who reviewed, who can stop? | | |

| Review | When and on which trigger is the sheet reviewed? | | |

## Counter-check {#sec-b27-countercheck}

A passport can be checked mechanically for the mismatches that matter most. The function below compares the target
statement with the split, the ID overlap, the unit of the headline result and the population the data come from.
Before running it, predict the number of findings for three passports: the teaching passport, the original abstract
(4/4 from plan 1), and the teaching passport with its target moved from new animals to patients.

```{r}
#| label: b27-review
review_passport <- function(p) {
  findings <- character(0)
  if (p$target_unit == "new animals" && p$split != "by animal")
    findings <- c(findings, "split does not create new animals")
  if (length(p$id_overlap) > 0)
    findings <- c(findings, "IDs overlap between training and test")
  if (p$target_unit %in% c("new animals", "patients") && p$headline_unit != "animal")
    findings <- c(findings, "headline counts spectra, target counts individuals")
  if (is.null(p$interval))
    findings <- c(findings, "no uncertainty interval")
  if (p$target_population != p$data_population)
    findings <- c(findings, "no data from the target population")
  findings
}

teaching <- list(target_unit = "new animals", split = "by animal", id_overlap = overlap2,
                 headline_unit = "animal", interval = exact_ci(1, 2),
                 target_population = "animals", data_population = "animals")
abstract_claim <- list(target_unit = "new animals", split = "by spectrum", id_overlap = overlap1,
                       headline_unit = "spectrum", interval = NULL,
                       target_population = "animals", data_population = "animals")
moved_target <- modifyList(teaching, list(target_unit = "patients", target_population = "patients"))

reviews <- lapply(list(teaching = teaching, abstract = abstract_claim, patients = moved_target), review_passport)
reviews
stopifnot(length(reviews$teaching) == 0, length(reviews$abstract) == 4,
          identical(reviews$patients, "no data from the target population"))
```

The teaching passport passes; the abstract fails on four counts that all come from the same decision, the split by
spectrum. Moving the target to patients produces a single finding, but it is the one no amount of re-analysis can fix:
the data contain no patients. Closing it requires a new study in the target population (@sec-b19), with its own
passport and its own decision sheet. Note what the function does not check: whether the reference standard is sound,
whether two test animals are enough, whether the classes are clinically meaningful. Those remain questions for the human
counter-review.

## Consequences for patients and operations {#sec-b27-consequences}

**Patients and animals.** In the teaching case no patient is affected yet, but the abstract is the point at which a
claim starts to travel. A "100% accuracy" that later justifies a first-in-human study would expose patients to a test
whose value was never shown in new individuals. On the animal side, an overstated result can trigger confirmatory
experiments that a careful passport would have redirected. A clear negative passport is therefore a contribution to
the 3Rs (@sec-b16).

**Regulation.** The passport and decision sheet are not the technical documentation required for a medical device or a
high-risk AI system; they are the research record from which such documentation could later be written. The
regulatory question changes with the intended purpose (@sec-b22). The decision sheet records the current purpose and
names the event – a planned clinical use – that would trigger a new assessment.

**Data protection and security.** Here both are minor because the data are synthetic and from animals. With human data,
the decision sheet refers to the legal basis, the access tier of every product (@sec-b26) and the checksum of the
evaluated artefact, so that the reported model is demonstrably the tested one (@sec-b25).

**Operations and responsibility.** A decision sheet without names is a wish list. Each line needs a role that exists in
the organisation, and the review date needs a trigger as well as a date. For a model in a running pilot, the decision
sheet is the place where the stop criterion and the person who may apply it are written down (@sec-b20).

## Look up and transfer {#sec-b27-lookup}

**Reviewer question:** Which entry of the passport would change if the target statement were "new patients" instead of
"new animals of the same species", and which evidence would then be required?

**Self-test:** A team reports a fracture alert with an assumed sensitivity and specificity of 90% each, evaluated at a
referral centre where 20 of 100 examined patients had a fracture. They want to write in the passport: "useful in our
emergency department", where 5 of 100 have a fracture (the scenario of @sec-b09). Which passport field is wrong, which
reporting path fits the evidence they have, and what would the decision sheet say?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The target statement does not match the data: the evidence comes from a population with 20% prevalence, the claim is
about one with 5%. With the same sensitivity and specificity, the positive predictive value falls from 180/260 (69.2%)
to 45/140 (32.1%), so roughly two of three alerts in the emergency department would concern patients without a
fracture. The evidence is diagnostic accuracy, so the reporting path is STARD-AI; a claim about usefulness in the
department needs an early clinical evaluation reported with DECIDE-AI. The decision sheet would allow at most a
supervised pilot without influence on treatment (for example in shadow mode, @sec-b20), name the clinical lead who
can stop it, and set a review after a fixed number of alerts.
:::

**Annotated sources**

- @sounderajah2025stardai – reporting guideline for diagnostic accuracy studies using AI (an erratum appeared in
  September 2026); the path for diagnostic claims.
- @collins2024tripodai – reporting guideline for prediction models using regression or machine learning; also the
  source of the model-side items in the animal short report.
- @moons2025probastai – appraisal tool for quality, risk of bias and applicability of prediction model studies.
- @vasey2022decideai – reporting guideline for the early clinical evaluation of AI decision support.
- @percie2020arrive – ARRIVE 2.0 with the Essential 10, the minimum for any report of animal research.
- @monks2019stress and @grimm2020odd – reporting of discrete-event, agent-based and system dynamics simulations, and
  the ODD protocol for agent-based models.
- @mitchell2019modelcards and @gebru2021datasheets – model cards and datasheets, the documentation formats the passport
  builds on.
- @kapoor2023leakage – survey of leakage in machine-learning-based science and the case for structured model
  information sheets.

## Further reading {#sec-b27-further}

- @sec-b19 – the split plan, ID checks and external tests behind the teaching passport.
- @sec-b07 – how to read a published AI study with the same guidelines.
- @sec-b16 – sample size, small denominators and the 3Rs for the next animal experiment.
- [Methods in R: Reporting templates](https://r-heller.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-reporting-index.html), in particular
  [TRIPOD-AI](https://r-heller.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-reporting-tripod-ai.html) and
  [ARRIVE](https://r-heller.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-reporting-arrive.html) – fill-in templates for the two
  guidelines of the short report.
- [Methods in R: Writing a report – Reporting guidelines](https://r-heller.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-appendices-d-writing-a-report.html#sec-appendices-d-writing-a-report-reporting-guidelines)
  – where guidelines fit into a manuscript.
- [CTTIR Courses: Writing a report](https://cttir.github.io/courses/appendices/writing_a_report.html) – IMRaD, effect
  sizes with intervals and reproducibility in one page.
- [CTTIR Courses: Pre-registration and statistical analysis plans](https://cttir.github.io/courses/course3_design_causal/labs/lab_week4_session5.html)
  – fixing the target statement and the analysis before the next experiment.
- [CTTIR Courses: TRIPOD-AI, fairness auditing, reproducibility at scale](https://cttir.github.io/courses/course4_ml_highdim/labs/lab_week4_session5.html)
  – a lab that walks through the reporting items of a prediction model.
